description: FireFuse is a solo team led by Zeynep Ceyhun, a high school AI/ML researcher working on medical imaging and health AI. We’re harmonizing 25 years of NASA MODIS and VIIRS fire hotspots into one consistent record, using a validated machine-learning model, and turning it into an interactive burning activity calendar for fire managers in Argentina. Skills: Python, machine learning, data science, remote sensing, web apps.
summary: FireFuse is a web app and AI method that merges NASA’s two fire-detection records into one consistent 25-year history for Argentina, the region of the challenge partner CONAE. MODIS has recorded fires since 2000 but is retiring. Its successor, VIIRS (2012 onward), has sharper 375 m pixels and sees about three times more fires, so joining the records creates a false jump in 2012 and about ten years of history would be lost. I gridded 4.6 million NASA FIRMS detections into 25 km monthly cells and trained a LightGBM model on the years both satellites overlap. It learns to convert MODIS counts into VIIRS-equivalent counts using fire intensity, neighbouring cells, season, location, viewing angle and land cover. I then applied it to 2001–2011, with an 80% uncertainty range on every value. On held-out years 2020–2025, error fell from 71% (raw MODIS) to 10%. I also found that Terra’s orbit drifted about an hour earlier after 2021, so the final model trains on stable years and reaches 5.6% error. The bilingual app lets fire teams pick an area, flag anomalies (Chilecito, July 2026: 10× normal), see season trends and download the data.
details:
What it does and how it works. MODIS (2000–) and VIIRS (2012–) detect fires differently, so their records can’t be joined. FireFuse learns the conversion. I aggregated about 4.6 million NASA FIRMS detections over Argentina into 0.25° (about 25 km) monthly cells, about 615,000 cell-months. For each cell I built features from MODIS: counts (total, Terra, Aqua, night), fire radiative power (sum, mean, max), the 3×3 neighbourhood, previous and next month, the cell’s seasonal climatology, latitude and longitude, month, viewing geometry, and ESA CCI land cover. A LightGBM model with a Poisson objective, trained on the stable-orbit overlap years 2012–2021, predicts the VIIRS count. A separate Terra-only model covers 2001 to mid-2002. I applied the model to MODIS-only 2001–2011 and quantified uncertainty with 10 bootstrap-by-year models, giving an 80% band on every value.

Validation. Train 2012–2019, test 2020–2025 against real VIIRS counts: national error was 71% for raw MODIS, 14% for simple ×3.2 scaling and 10.0% for FireFuse (regional R² 0.93). I found that Terra’s overpass time drifted about an hour earlier after 2021, so the final model trains on stable years and reaches 5.6% error. Land cover and viewing angle each reduced error; overpass-time features were rejected. The 2008 Paraná Delta fires appear in the harmonized record, four years before VIIRS existed.

Benefits and intended impact. Fire managers (for example, CONAE) get one consistent record to see whether a month is normal for an area. Chilecito, July 2026 had 150 hotspots against a historical July median of 15. Scientists get 25 years that can be compared without the false 2012 jump, and the same method can run wherever FIRMS has data, which protects NASA’s long record as MODIS retires.

The app. Pick an area by preset, map click or lat/lon box, then see a calendar, anomalies, season trends, the fires MODIS alone missed, and a CSV download, in English and Spanish.

Tools. Python, pandas, LightGBM, scikit-learn, SciPy, Streamlit, Folium, Plotly, Google Colab, Microsoft Planetary Computer, GitHub.

Creativity and factors considered. The framing treats this as sensor calibration, an idea from medical imaging where different scanners must be harmonized, rather than as fire prediction. I considered cost (free data and a free-tier host), accessibility (bilingual, in-browser, no installation), and honesty about uncertainty (80% bands and stated limits).

Limitations. Validated on Argentina only; 2001–2011 can’t be tested directly because VIIRS didn’t exist; counts are detections, not burned area.

Use of AI. AI assistance (Claude by Anthropic) was used to help build the Streamlit frontend. The frontend is labeled “SI-generated” in the app, and the slides carry the same label.

The following are my own work: the problem framing, the feature design, the LightGBM model, the validation, the orbit-drift analysis, the interpretation of results, and the Colab notebook (data processing, model training and analysis).

No SI-generated images, video or audio were used, and no NASA logos or branding appear in this project. All data come from NASA FIRMS (MODIS C6.1 and VIIRS S-NPP 375 m) and ESA CCI Land Cover, listed in the data section.
